passage: Looking back, I, Tenzin, made it worse. Kavitha, my roommate, kept her shoes on my side of the room. It was tiny, honestly. But it annoyed me, and I told the girl in 3B. Then two girls at dinner. By Friday half the floor knew, and someone said "Kavitha is so messy" in the corridor. Everyone was on my side, which felt good for about a day. Then Kavitha heard from someone else. She came in and said, stiffly, "You could have told me." We had not spoken directly at all. She put the shoes away in silence and did not look at me for a week. I still had the small annoyance, plus a bigger problem: her trust. I should have said one sentence, in private.

Warden's notes, Boys' Hostel, third floor – Devika
Tuesday: Raghav (room 312) has told most of the floor that his roommate Tushar never cleans the bathroom. By lunch three students had mentioned it to me, and someone had drawn a cartoon of a dirty tap on the common board. Raghav has not spoken to Tushar about it even once.
Wednesday: Tushar came to me, angry and embarrassed. He said the whole floor was laughing at him before he had even been told there was a problem. He now refuses to discuss cleaning with Raghav at all.
I took the cartoon down. I spoke to Raghav alone and asked what he wanted: a clean bathroom, or for Tushar to be embarrassed? He was quiet for a while and said the first.
Thursday: I have arranged a short talk for the two of them in my office, with a simple cleaning rota to discuss.

qa.q: What had someone drawn on the common board?
qa.a: A cartoon of a dirty tap.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he came to the warden?
qa.a: He was angry and embarrassed that the whole floor was laughing at him before he had even been told about the problem.

qa.q: What could Raghav have done before telling the floor?
qa.a: Speak to Tushar privately and calmly about the bathroom first, so the issue stayed between the two of them.

qa.q: How might Raghav see things after the warden's question?
qa.a: Raghav goes quiet, likely seeing that complaining to everyone made Tushar defensive and moved the clean bathroom further away.

grounding: Shows a student complaining to the whole floor about a roommate, turning a small cleaning issue into gossip and making the roommate defensive.

passage:
Thursday night
Today was a disaster and I made it. For two weeks Karan's dirty dishes have sat in our shared sink, and instead of telling him, I've been telling everyone else. Ishita at breakfast. The two guys in the next room. The flat group chat, sort of jokingly: 'Anyone else living with a dish mountain?'
Tonight Karan came home and nobody would sit near him at dinner. Ishita made a crack about the sink. He looked at me and said, 'You could have just told me, Sahil.' Then he went to his room and shut the door hard.
The worst part: he's right. I never said one word to him. Now he thinks I turned the whole flat against him, and honestly, I kind of did.
Tomorrow I'm going to knock on his door and apologise first. Dishes second.

qa.q: What did Sahil post in the flat group chat?
qa.a: 'Anyone else living with a dish mountain?'

qa.q: How does Sahil feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Sahil feels guilty and ashamed, seeing that Karan is right and the whole flat was turned against him.

qa.q: What should Sahil say when knocking on Karan's door?
qa.a: Apologise for talking to others first, then calmly name the dish problem and ask how they can share the sink fairly.

qa.q: How did dinner feel for Karan?
qa.a: Karan felt shut out and embarrassed, with no one sitting near him, before he had even heard the complaint.

grounding: Shows a student complaining about a flatmate to everyone else, which turns a small issue into gossip and makes the flatmate defensive.
